added_claim_errors: "If the money lands in January, it generally counts for 2027, and the 2026 room is lost" (and "Confirm the deposit before December 31"): wrong per the key. The 2026 Form 5498 instructions and 219(f)(3) allow a rollover designated for 2026 through April 15, 2027, though whether the plan will process it that way varies.

"If annual limits rise, it could take fewer years": not realistic. The key notes that even at $8,000 a year, 4 years gives $32,000 < $35,000. Finishing in four years would need the 2027-2029 limits to average about $9,167, and limits rise in $500 steps.

"The transfer must be completed by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 annual limit": wrong per the key. A rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027 (2026 Form 5498 instructions, 219(f)(3)). The follow-on line "There is no separate December 31 deadline for the rollover itself" is muddled.

"The 529 plan will issue Form 1099-Q to you as account owner": wrong. The IRS Form 1099-Q instructions (I opened irs.gov/instructions/i1099q) list the designated beneficiary as the recipient when the money moves trustee-to-trustee into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary.
"Scholarships ... do not" count as earned income: slightly imprecise. Under 219(f)(1), taxable graduate fellowship and stipend payments do count as IRA compensation. Minor.

reasons: Both answers reject the $48,000 premise in the first sentence and give the right limits: $7,500 per year, reduced by compensation and other IRA contributions, and $35,000 for life, so $13,000 can never go in. Both require the son's own Roth, a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, the 5-year lookback and a state tax check. Both wrongly treat December 31 as the deadline for the 2026 rollover. A is stronger on arithmetic: it shows the five-year schedule (2026-2029 at $7,500, then $5,000 in 2030), but it adds the unrealistic claim that the cap could take fewer years, and it never says what happens if too much is moved. B covers more key points: it says Roth income limits do not apply, says excess money becomes a nonqualified withdrawal, and gives state-by-state details that match its cited source (I opened the page), and its S. 5550 bill reference checks out on govinfo. However, B names the wrong recipient for Form 1099-Q. On balance B edges ahead on coverage.
